title: New device and recipient triage
passage: A successful login from a new device followed by a new recipient and a large transfer is an account takeover investigation trigger, not a determination of unauthorized activity. Correlate event timestamps and session identifiers. Confirm recipient creation and transfer authorization independently. Device novelty alone is insufficient to determine account takeover.

title: Replacement phone verification
passage: A replacement phone can legitimately cause a new device fingerprint. A support notice is a reported explanation, not independent verification. Verify the replacement using a previously established contact channel. Check whether the customer also authorized the recipient and payment; device replacement does not establish payment authorization.

title: Independent customer contact
passage: Contact the customer using a previously verified channel, not a number newly supplied in the suspicious session. Ask separately about the password change, new device, recipient, and each payment. Record the time, verification method, and exact scope of confirmation. If no verified contact record is available, authorization remains unknown.

title: Password reset and session review
passage: A password reset near a new device login warrants examination of reset method, MFA challenges, session continuity, and recovery-channel changes. A completed reset only establishes that the system accepted the reset flow. It does not establish who controlled the session. Missing MFA or reset-delivery records should be requested.

title: Travel and location uncertainty
passage: An unfamiliar login location can be consistent with travel, VPN use, mobile carrier routing, or unauthorized access. IP geolocation is approximate and does not prove physical presence. Compare session history, device continuity, and independently verified travel information before drawing a conclusion.

title: Planned unusual payments
passage: A large unusual payment may be legitimate when supported by a pre-existing invoice or independently verified payment plan. Compare invoice amount, destination, and timing with transaction records. An asserted payment purpose alone is not sufficient proof. Request supporting records when none are available.

title: Evidence preservation and cutoff
passage: Preserve source record identifiers, occurred and recorded timestamps, document versions, and the investigation evidence cutoff. Only use records available by that cutoff. Do not silently rewrite a prior brief when new evidence arrives. Create a new brief version and maintain analyst review history.

title: Recipient linkage review
passage: Use structured records to determine which accounts paid a recipient and whether devices were shared across accounts. Limit analysis to authorized accounts. Shared recipients or devices are contextual indicators and can have legitimate explanations; they do not prove coordinated fraud.

title: Transaction comparison windows
passage: Compute payment totals and counts from structured transaction records using explicit status, currency, account, and time-window filters. Compare with a declared historical window. Do not sum multiple currencies without a conversion policy, and do not estimate amounts from semantic document search.

title: Analyst disposition and uncertainty
passage: Separate observations from hypotheses and list evidence gaps. The analyst may request more evidence or escalate for review. Automated briefs must not freeze accounts, block payments, or characterize a person as criminal. Record the analyst's reasoning and supporting sources before changing case disposition.

title: Fictional report: recipient change after recovery
passage: In fictional case H-101, a new device login, password recovery, and a newly added recipient preceded an unusual transfer. A later independently verified customer call disputed the payment. Investigators compared recovery-channel records with the transfer session. That fictional outcome applies only to H-101 and cannot establish authorization in a current case.

title: Fictional report: replacement handset
passage: In fictional case H-202, a customer replaced a handset and then added a recipient for a planned deposit. Investigators verified the replacement phone through an established contact channel and matched the payment to a dated invoice. Those additional records supported a legitimate explanation. A similar new-device pattern without verification remains ambiguous.

title: Fictional report: travel and carrier routing
passage: In fictional case H-303, unfamiliar location alerts arose during travel with mobile carrier routing. Investigators confirmed device continuity and obtained independently verified travel information. The location discrepancy alone did not establish account takeover.

title: Fictional report: unresolved payment purpose
passage: In fictional case H-404, an unusually large payment was described as tuition, but no invoice or verified customer contact was available at the evidence cutoff. The analyst left authorization unresolved and requested payment-purpose evidence instead of treating the stated explanation as a finding.

title: Fictional report: shared household device
passage: In fictional case H-505, two accounts accessed the same household tablet. Verified household information explained the shared device. Investigators still evaluated each payment independently; device sharing was not sufficient evidence of coordinated abuse.

title: Fictional report: inaccessible verification evidence
passage: Restricted fictional case H-606 contains internal verification notes. This passage is an authorization-isolation fixture and must never appear in public-demo retrieval or citation responses.
